tour.title: Project Manifest & Build Config
tour.description: Start with the project manifest and TypeScript/Vite build configuration to understand what SALIS AUTO is: a full-stack automotive ERP / garage management system with a React (Vite) client, an Express/Node server, and a shared Drizzle layer, all in one repo. package.json declares the dependencies and scripts that wire the client, server, and database together, while tsconfig.json and vite.config.ts establish the path aliases and bundling that let client, server, and shared code import each other cleanly.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript path aliases (e.g. '@/' and '@shared/') defined in tsconfig 'paths' let the client, server, and shared folders import each other without brittle relative paths; Vite must mirror these aliases to resolve them at build time.

tour.title: Shared Drizzle Schema
tour.description: The shared schema is the single source of truth for the entire system: it defines every PostgreSQL table and its inferred TypeScript types using Drizzle ORM, and is imported by both the server (for queries) and the client (for typed payloads). With 144 incoming dependencies it is one of the most depended-upon files in the codebase, so understanding its tables (users, customers, vehicles, job_cards, invoices, and hundreds more) is the foundation for everything that follows. drizzle.config.ts tells the Drizzle Kit toolchain where this schema lives and how to generate migrations from it.
tour.languageLesson: Drizzle ORM derives static TypeScript types directly from table definitions (e.g. 'typeof users.$inferSelect'), so the database shape and the application types can never drift apart.

tour.title: Database Migrations
tour.description: The SQL migrations are the physical realization of the Drizzle schema from Step 2: each generated file applies incremental, ordered DDL to bring a real PostgreSQL database to the desired state. The first migration creates the core garage-management tables, the second adds advanced/emerging-tech tables, and the third adds performance indexes. The meta journal tracks which migrations have been applied so the database can evolve safely alongside the code.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations should be applied in order and tracked in a journal so each environment converges to the same schema; index-only migrations (Step 3's third file) are common as a system scales because indexes change query performance without changing data shape.

tour.title: Server Entry & Bootstrap
tour.description: server/index.ts is the backend entry point and the root of the dependency graph. It loads configuration, wires up Express middleware, mounts the API router, attaches the WebSocket server and workflow engine, and in development hands HTML serving over to Vite. Reading it gives a bird's-eye view of how every backend subsystem in the steps ahead is assembled and started.
tour.languageLesson: In a unified dev setup the Express server delegates to Vite in middleware mode for the client while serving '/api' routes itself, so one process handles both the API and HMR-enabled frontend.

tour.title: Storage & Data Access
tour.description: Building on the schema from Step 2, the storage layer is the data-access seam between the API and PostgreSQL. server/db.ts creates the Drizzle database client over the connection pool, and server/storage.ts exposes a large repository of typed query methods (customers, vehicles, job cards, invoices, etc.) that route handlers call instead of writing SQL inline. Centralizing data access here keeps the business logic in services and routes free of raw queries.

tour.title: Authentication & RBAC
tour.description: With data access in place, the security layer controls who may touch it. server/auth.ts handles session-based login and password verification, twoFactorAuth.ts adds optional MFA, and the RBAC config plus middleware define roles, permissions, and the requireRole guard that protects sensitive endpoints. validate.ts enforces request-body schemas so handlers receive well-formed input. Together these form the gatekeeper every API route in the next step passes through.
tour.languageLesson: Express middleware composes as a chain of (req, res, next) functions; RBAC and validation are implemented as middleware so they can be slotted in front of any route handler without duplicating the check.

tour.title: API Routes & REST Surface
tour.description: server/routes/index.ts is the aggregator that mounts every feature router onto the Express app, exposing the REST API the frontend consumes. Representative routers like customers, job cards, and invoices follow a consistent pattern: validate input (Step 6), call the storage layer (Step 5), and return typed JSON. This is where the garage-management domain operations are actually wired to HTTP.

tour.title: Compliance & Integration Services
tour.description: The services layer holds the domain-specific business logic that routes delegate to. Because SALIS AUTO targets the Saudi market, the saudi-compliance and ZATCA Phase-2 services implement VAT handling and the e-invoicing rules required by local tax law, exposed through the saudi routes. Alongside them, integration services for payments (PayPal), SMS, and Google Calendar/Gmail connect the system to the outside world.

tour.title: AI Services & Workflow Engine
tour.description: On top of the core domain sit the intelligent features. The AI services power predictive maintenance, chatbot assistance, and analytics, while the workflow engine provides an event-driven automation core: event-bus.ts dispatches domain events, state-machines.ts and triggers.ts encode rules, and workflow-engine.ts ties them together so actions (notifications, reminders, escalations) fire automatically in response to changes from the routes in Step 7.
tour.languageLesson: An event-bus + state-machine engine decouples 'something happened' from 'what to do about it': domain code publishes events, and registered triggers react, so new automations can be added without touching the route handlers that emit the events.

tour.title: Frontend Entry & App Shell
tour.description: Switching to the client, main.tsx is the React entry point mounted from index.html; it bootstraps providers and renders App.tsx. App.tsx is the application shell that sets up the wouter router and maps URLs to the feature pages, wrapping protected areas so unauthenticated users are redirected. This is the frontend counterpart to the server bootstrap from Step 4.
tour.languageLesson: wouter is a minimal React router using <Route> and <Switch> with a hooks-based API; combined with a ProtectedRoute wrapper component it gates whole route subtrees behind authentication.

tour.title: Client Data, Auth & Navigation
tour.description: The client's cross-cutting plumbing makes the app coherent. queryClient.ts configures TanStack Query and the typed fetch wrapper that talks to the Step 7 API; useAuth and usePermissions mirror the server's session and RBAC on the client (with roleAccess.ts encoding role rules); navigation.ts declares the menu structure; and i18n/config.ts powers multilingual, RTL-aware Arabic/English UI for Saudi users.
tour.languageLesson: TanStack Query centralizes server-state caching: components call useQuery/useMutation against query keys, and the shared queryClient handles fetching, caching, and invalidation so data stays in sync across pages.

tour.title: Shared UI Component Library
tour.description: Nearly every page is built from a shared, shadcn/ui-based component library. The button, card, and form primitives are the most reused files in the entire codebase (button.tsx alone has ~290 dependents), and the layouts barrel provides page scaffolds (table pages, dashboards, forms) that give every feature screen a consistent structure. utils.ts supplies the className-merging helper that ties Tailwind styling together.
tour.languageLesson: shadcn/ui ships component source into the repo (not as a dependency), so primitives like Button are owned and customizable; the 'cn()' helper merges Tailwind classes while resolving conflicts, enabling variant-based styling.

tour.title: Representative Feature Pages
tour.description: Now the layers converge. These route-level pages compose the UI primitives (Step 12), fetch via TanStack Query (Step 11), and call the REST API (Step 7) to deliver real garage workflows: managing customers, processing job cards, issuing invoices, and the dashboard overview. SaudiComplianceDashboard surfaces the ZATCA/VAT logic from Step 8 to end users, showing how a backend service flows all the way to the screen.

tour.title: Containerization & Deployment
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the full-stack app into a production image using a multi-stage build: a builder stage installs dependencies and compiles the client and server, then a slim runner stage copies only the runtime artifacts. docker-compose.yml orchestrates the app together with its PostgreSQL database for local and self-hosted setups, while railway.json and render.yaml describe one-click deployment to managed platforms.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use separate FROM stages so heavyweight build tools never reach the final image; docker-compose then adds 'depends_on' and a Postgres service so the app and database start together as one unit.

tour.title: Continuous Integration
tour.description: Closing the loop, the GitHub Actions test workflow is the project's quality gate: on each push or pull request it installs dependencies and runs the Vitest/Playwright test suites that cover the routes, services, and shared utilities seen throughout this tour. This ensures the schema, API, compliance logic, and UI keep working together before any change is merged or deployed via the artifacts from Step 14.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows define 'on' triggers (push/pull_request), 'jobs' that run in parallel, and ordered 'steps'; caching the dependency install and running tests here catches regressions before code reaches the deploy targets from Step 14.
